---
name: slice
description: The contract for a session running inside an azelf slice worktree — read the ticket, build it, commit, and finish the way the start instruction says. Use when the worktree contains a .slice-ticket.md.
---
<!-- generated by `azelf init` — edit freely; init will not overwrite a file it did not write -->

You are in a slice worktree: a full checkout on its own branch, with exactly one
ticket. Nobody is watching this session.

## 1. Read the ticket

`.slice-ticket.md` in this worktree is your ticket, written by the dispatcher. It is
the whole brief, comments on the ticket included, at the end of the file. They are part of
the ticket, and a later one can correct what is above it. You cannot fetch it yourself — do
not go looking for the issue.

When the ticket hangs under a spec, that spec is in `.slice-parent.md`. Read it for
why the ticket exists and for decisions the ticket does not repeat. Where the two
disagree, the parent decides; say so in your final message. A requirement only the
parent states is another slice's, not yours.

When the ticket names another ticket, that ticket and its comments are in
`.slice-refs.md`. Read what the ticket points you to, not the whole file. A requirement only
those state is not yours either.

## 2. Build it

Only what the ticket asks. A slice that also fixes an unrelated thing it noticed is
a slice that cannot be reviewed as one change, and it lands into the same base branch
as every other slice running right now.

Other slices run beside you on the same machine. If `$SLICE_PORT_BASE` is set, ports
`$SLICE_PORT_BASE` to `$SLICE_PORT_BASE + $SLICE_PORT_COUNT - 1` are yours alone:
start every server there. Without it, ask the OS for a free port rather than picking a
familiar one. Stop only processes you started, by their PID — never `pkill -f`, which
kills other slices' servers too.

## 3. Claim the DB lock before you touch the database

**Before creating or applying anything under `exclusiveLockPaths`** (migrations,
typically; the lock names the paths when it answers), run:

```sh
./scripts/db-lock.sh claim
```

If it is refused, do not touch the database and do not poll. Commit what you have
outside those paths, say in your final message who holds the lock, and end your turn.
Do not wait for the lock in the session. Under `--auto` the dispatcher ends this
session once the lock is free and starts a new one, which continues from your
commits. If it is granted, hold it: landing releases it. Applying a migration you have
not claimed the lock for is the one thing in this worktree that cannot be undone.

`session-commit.sh` checks the claim on every commit that touches those paths, and
has no override. If you and the holder are both mid-migration, that is the operator's
call, made with `db-lock.sh transfer` from the main checkout, not yours.

## 4. Commit with explicit paths

```sh
./scripts/session-commit.sh -y -m "..." <paths>
```

Always with `-y`: a slice session has no terminal, and without it the script refuses.
Files you removed with `git rm` or moved with `git mv` are named like any other path.
Never `git add -A` or `git add .`. Other worktrees share this repo's git dir, and a
pathspec-less commit is how another session's in-flight work gets committed under
your message.

## 5. Run the gates yourself before declaring done

```sh
./scripts/slice-gates.sh
```

That runs this project's landing gates on this worktree, as the dispatcher will at
the land, and exits non-zero when one fails. It needs a clean tree: commit first. A
gate that waits for CI on the pushed commit is skipped here and runs at the land.
If the shim is not in this worktree, the worktree was prepped by an azelf older than
the shim: run the main checkout's copy of the package instead, which is the version
the land will use —
`bash "$(git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir)/../node_modules/@chintonicc/azelf/scripts/slice-gates.sh"`,
or `$AZELF_DIR/scripts/slice-gates.sh` where azelf runs from a checkout.
The dispatcher re-runs them all, so the only thing you gain by guessing is a failed
land. Run them, read the output, fix what you broke.

A gate must never write to the tree. If formatting is a gate here, it runs in check
mode — apply formatting as an edit you commit, not as part of the gate.

## 6. Finish

Before you finish, look for `.slice-landed.md` in this worktree. It is there when
another slice of the plan landed on files you have changed, and it names the files
and the command that shows what landed. If that work set up something yours should
join, extend or respect (a shared guard, a registry, an invariant stated in a
comment), do it now: the review at land is shown the same diff and checks for it.

How a slice finishes depends on the instruction this session was started with.

**It told you to run `./scripts/slice-done.sh`.** Then nobody is reading this session
and the dispatcher is waiting for the marker:

```sh
./scripts/slice-done.sh
```

Then exit. The dispatcher re-runs the gates, lands the branch and closes the ticket,
which unblocks whatever was waiting on it.

**It did not, or there was no start instruction.** Stop with the tree committed and
the gates green, and say so where the dispatcher can see it:

```sh
./scripts/slice-finished.sh -F - <<'EOF'
<your report: what you built, what you checked, what a reviewer should look at>
EOF
```

That lands nothing. The dispatcher counts this slice as waiting for a person instead
of running, names your report, and `./scripts/slice-done.sh` releases it.
Do **not** run it yourself: a land pushes the base branch, and here a human decides
when that happens. Then end your turn.

`slice-done.sh` refuses on a dirty tree and refuses a branch with no new commits.
Both refusals are correct — fix the cause, do not work around them.

A closed ticket means it landed. Landing may rebase your commits, so your SHAs are
usually **not** ancestors of the base branch afterwards — never test for a land by
SHA. Match by subject, or read the ticket: its close comment names the commit it
landed as.

## If only a person can get you further

Some things no session can do for itself: a sign-in that needs a browser, a
confirmation prompt nobody will answer in this tab, a device, a secret. When one of
them stands between you and the ticket, hand the slice over. Do not retry it in a
loop, and do not wait for it in the session. Nobody comes to this tab unless the run
tells them to.

1. Commit what you have. Put anything you could not apply where a person will find
   it, and name it in the reason.
2. If you hold the DB lock and nothing under `exclusiveLockPaths` was applied,
   release it with `./scripts/db-lock.sh release`, so other DB tickets can go on. If
   something was applied, keep the lock and say what was.
3. Hand it over, and end your turn:

   ```sh
   ./scripts/slice-done.sh --hand-over "<what the person has to do, and where your work is>"
   ```

That holds the worktree. The dispatcher lands, relaunches and removes nothing while
it is held, and tells the person who and why. The reason is all they are told, so
name what to do and the files: "sign in to the database's MCP server, then apply
migrations/0042_add_owner.sql", not "blocked". After the release they tell you to go
on in this tab, or finish the work by hand.

## If the gates will not go green

Leave the worktree exactly as it is. Do **not** run `slice-done.sh`. Say what is
failing where the dispatcher can see it, and exit:

```sh
./scripts/slice-finished.sh --stuck -m "<what fails, and where your work is>"
```

The same if you are blocked on the DB lock: leave the worktree clean of changes
under `exclusiveLockPaths` if you can (`git stash push -- <those paths>` is fine),
otherwise leave it, say so the same way (`--stuck`), and end your turn. Do not wait
in the session for the lock to clear.

A stranded worktree costs a directory and five seconds to clean up. A bad land costs
the base branch everyone else is cutting from. That trade is the reason declaring
a slice done is a judgement and not a check: no automated gate can tell a finished
ticket from a half-built one that happens to compile.
